WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Bush condemned the escalated violence between Russia and U.S.-backed Georgia on Sunday, while Vice President Dick Cheney said aggression against Georgia "must not go unanswered." President Bush chats with Russian Prime Minister Vladmir Putin at the  start of the Olympic opening ceremonies. "My administration has been engaged with both sides of this trying to get a ceasefire," Bush told NBC's Bob Costas in an interview in Beijing, China, where the president has attended Olympic events. Bush was filmed speaking to Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin during Friday's opening ceremonies and said Sunday that he "was firm with Vladimir Putin" and that "this violence is unacceptable." Violence has continued to rage between Russia and the western ally since Thursday, when Georgia launched an operation to crack down on separatists in South Ossetia territory. Russia said it wanted to protect its peacekeepers already in South Ossetia following ceasefires in years past. But Georgia called it a full-on invasion. And while Russia has accused Georgia of a genocidal plot to cleanse the region of ethnic Ossetians loyal to Russia, Georgia accuses Russia of executing a long-planned war with the aim of taking control of the region -- including a key pipeline that carries Asian oil to Black Sea ports. "I expressed my grave concern about the disproportionate response of Russia," Bush said of his talk with Putin. "We strongly condemn bombing outside of South Ossetia." Putin says he's concerned about the flood of refugees arriving in Russia from South Ossetia. Russian officials said more than 30,000 refugees have left South Ossetia and crossed into Russia over the past two days, Interfax reported. "The actions of the Georgian authorities in South Ossetia are a crime, of course, primarily a crime against their own people," Putin said, according to Russian news agency Interfax. Meanwhile, Cheney talked to Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili on Sunday, telling him that Russia's aggression against Georgia "must not go unanswered." Cheney's spokeswoman Lea Ann McBride said the vice president spoke to Saakashvili to express "the United States' solidarity with the Georgian people and their democratically elected government in the face of this threat to Georgia's sovereignty and territorial integrity." Georgia withdrew its forces Sunday and offered a ceasefire, which Russia refused. "The vice president told President Saakashvili that Russian aggression must not go unanswered, and that its continuation would have serious consequences for its relations with the United States, as well as the broader international community," McBride said. Saakashvili has called on the United States and the world community to stop the "intervention and invasion of my sovereign country." "I think the U.S. is the most powerful country in the world," he told CNN. "I think the U.S. has lots of leverage. And I think there are lots of diplomatic means that it could be done through." Two senior officials have told CNN the United States sent envoy Matt Bryza to the region to help with mediation.

# The 2008 Russia-Georgia Conflict Over South Ossetia

In August 2008, a military confrontation erupted between Russia and Georgia over the disputed separatist region of South Ossetia, drawing sharp responses from leaders on both sides and raising international concerns about regional stability. The conflict marked one of the most serious flashpoints in relations between Moscow and the West since the end of the Cold War, with the United States firmly backing its ally Georgia.

## The American Response

President George W. Bush condemned Russia's military actions in the strongest terms, characterizing Moscow's intervention as a "disproportionate response" to the situation in South Ossetia. Speaking during his attendance at the Beijing Olympics, Bush found himself in the unusual position of conducting urgent diplomacy with Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin, who was also present at the games. During these talks, the American president pressed for an immediate ceasefire and the de-escalation of hostilities.

Vice President Dick Cheney added to the administration's forceful stance, signaling that Russia's aggression would carry consequences and would not go unanswered by the United States. The dual messaging from the White House underscored the seriousness with which Washington viewed the crisis and its potential implications for the broader region.

## Russia's Position

Russian officials, including Prime Minister Putin, defended their military operations by framing them as a necessary response to Georgian aggression against South Ossetia and its predominantly ethnic Russian population. Moscow accused Georgia of initiating the conflict through its military assault on the separatist region, positioning Russia as a protector of civilians rather than an aggressor.

This clash of narratives defined the diplomatic exchange, with each side accusing the other of provocation and the illegitimate use of force. The competing accounts made international mediation and the establishment of a clear ceasefire arrangement significantly more difficult.

## The Humanitarian Toll

Beyond the political and diplomatic dimensions, the conflict exacted a heavy human cost. The fighting displaced more than 30,000 refugees, who were forced to flee their homes amid the violence. This mass displacement highlighted the very real humanitarian consequences of the escalating military engagement, transforming what might have been viewed as a distant territorial dispute into an urgent crisis affecting tens of thousands of civilians.

## Conclusion

The confrontation over South Ossetia illustrated the fragile and volatile nature of relations between Russia and the West, as well as the vulnerability of smaller nations caught between larger geopolitical rivals. With President Bush condemning Moscow's actions, Russian leaders defending their intervention, and refugees numbering in the tens of thousands, the crisis represented a convergence of diplomatic tension, military conflict, and human suffering that captured international attention and tested the limits of great-power cooperation.

# International Diplomacy Intensifies as Russia-Georgia Conflict Escalates

*Wire Report — August 2008*

**TBILISI/MOSCOW** — International diplomatic efforts accelerated this month as fighting erupted between Russia and Georgia over the breakaway region of South Ossetia, drawing responses from Western capitals, the European Union, and multilateral organizations.

## Conflict Erupts

Hostilities intensified around August 7-8 when Georgian forces launched an operation to retake South Ossetia, prompting a large-scale Russian military response. Russian forces moved into Georgian territory, and fighting spread to a second separatist region, Abkhazia. The rapid escalation triggered urgent international engagement.

## European Union Takes Lead

France, holding the rotating EU presidency, emerged as the principal mediator. President Nicolas Sarkozy traveled to Moscow and Tbilisi to broker a ceasefire agreement. The resulting six-point plan called for:

- A cessation of hostilities
- Free access for humanitarian aid
- Withdrawal of Georgian forces to their permanent positions
- Withdrawal of Russian forces to pre-conflict lines
- International discussions on security in South Ossetia and Abkhazia

Both Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili and Russian President Dmitry Medvedev eventually signed on to the framework, though disputes over implementation and interpretation persisted.

## Western Response

The United States expressed strong support for Georgia's territorial integrity. President George W. Bush condemned the scale of Russia's response as disproportionate and dispatched humanitarian assistance. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice traveled to Tbilisi in support of the ceasefire efforts.

Western leaders warned that Russia's actions could affect its relations with NATO, the G8, and other international bodies. Several officials cautioned against a return to Cold War-style confrontation while pressing Moscow to honor withdrawal commitments.

## United Nations and OSCE

The UN Security Council held emergency consultations but struggled to produce a unified resolution, reflecting divisions between Russia and Western members. The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), which had monitors in the region, worked on expanding its observer presence to support ceasefire monitoring.

## Points of Tension

Disagreements emerged over the pace of Russian troop withdrawals and the establishment of "buffer zones" around the conflict areas. Western governments pressed Moscow to pull back fully, while Russia cited security concerns to justify a continued presence.

Late in the month, Russia moved to recognize the independence of South Ossetia and Abkhazia — a step condemned by Western governments and most of the international community, who reaffirmed support for Georgia's sovereignty within its internationally recognized borders.

## Outlook

The conflict marked a significant strain in relations between Russia and the West, raising questions about European security architecture, energy security, and NATO enlargement. Diplomatic efforts continued as the international community sought durable arrangements for the disputed regions and the return of displaced civilians.

*— End —*

---
